summary: Ezekiel 29 (21 verses) continues the story of glory. Starting with 'In the tenth year, in the tenth month, on the twelfth day of the month, Yahweh’s word came to me, saying,', it moves through themes of glory, idolatry and calls readers toward new heart.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows glory lived out in chebar canal, babylon. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: In the tenth year, in the tenth month, on the twelfth day of the month, Yahweh’s word came to me, saying,
No foot of man will pass through it, nor will any animal foot pass through it. It won’t be inhabited for forty years.
“In that day I will cause a horn to sprout for the house of Israel, and I will open your mouth among them. Then they will know that I am Yahweh.”

questions.question: What is happening in Ezekiel 29?
questions.answer: In 21 verses, this chapter ezekiel 29 (21 verses) continues the story of glory. starting with 'in the tenth year, in the tenth month, on the twelfth day of the month, yahweh’s word came to me, saying,', it moves through themes of glory, idolatry and calls readers toward new heart. The setting is chebar canal, babylon, written to exiles in babylon. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Ezekiel and why 29 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally ezekiel, addressed to exiles in babylon around ~593-571 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as visions, oracles — its themes of glory, idolatry build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'kingdom' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: God's reign/ rule. In this chapter, it appears in context of glory. For a first-time reader: think of it as god's reign/ rule, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through glory and idolatry, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 12 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'I will make the land of Egypt a desolation in the middle of the countries that are desolate. Her cities among the cities that are laid waste will be a desolation forty years. I wil...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about glory. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
